title: Chukat: Miriam's well (Numbers 20:1–2)
hookLine: Miriam dies and the water stops; the Talmud says a well went with them for her sake (Taanit 9a)

lines: THE ONE WHO HELD IT TOGETHER.
cards: Some people hold a family together so quietly that nobody notices until they're gone. The grandmother whose kitchen was where everyone ended up. The coworker who refilled the coffee and remembered birthdays.

After the funeral, something stops working, and only then does everyone realize who was doing it. The Torah has a verse like that. In one short line, Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, dies and is buried.
And in the very next line, there's no water.

teach.h: SHE DIED; THERE WAS NO WATER.
teach.b: The Torah's words are spare. In paraphrase: the people came to the wilderness of Zin and stayed at Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried there. Then: there was no water for the congregation.

That's all. No weeping is recorded for her, no days of mourning, nothing like what the Torah will record for Aaron and later for Moses. But the rabbis read the two verses together and heard something.
In the Talmud, tractate Taanit, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda teaches that three good leaders rose up for Israel: Moses, Aaron and Miriam.
And three good gifts came through them: the manna, for Moses' sake; the clouds of glory, for Aaron's sake; and the well, for Miriam's sake.

A well of water traveled with the people through the desert, the rabbis say, because of her. When she died, the well went dry, and that's why the very next verse says there was no water. Why Miriam and water?
Look at her story. As a girl, tradition says, she was the sister who stood by the Nile, watching her baby brother float in a basket among the reeds.

At the Sea, she took a timbrel and led the women in song after they crossed the water. Water follows her all the way through. The Torah never mentions a well; this is the rabbis reading between two verses.
But the picture has stayed. Today some families set a cup of water for Miriam on their Passover table. The well was her quiet gift.
Nobody named it while it flowed.

how: Miriam's death is read in synagogue as part of the portion of Chukat; today some families place a cup of water for Miriam, called Miriam's cup, on the Passover seder table.

o: statute: the portion where Miriam dies
the clouds of glory that came for Aaron
the wilderness of Zin, where Miriam died

games.q: three leaders, three gifts — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah describes Miriam's well in detail
the Torah never mentions a well. the rabbis read it from two verses: Miriam died, then there was no water.
the Torah describes the people mourning Miriam
it records only that she died and was buried. no mourning is described.
Miriam led the women in song at the Sea
she took a timbrel and the women followed her, singing (Exodus 15:20–21).

games.q: you're a rabbi reading Numbers 20. Miriam dies in verse one, and in verse two there's no water. what do you make of it?
o: the water came because of her, and left with her.
games.why: the Talmud reads it as a well that traveled with Israel for Miriam's sake, and stopped when she died.

practice: Ask yourself who has been a well in your life, someone who kept things flowing without asking for credit: a parent, a teacher, a neighbor, a friend who always checked in. If they're living, think how you might thank them.
If they've died, hold their name for a few breaths, and say it quietly if you'd like.

wordCard.voice: Chukat. The portion where Miriam dies, the water stops, and the rabbis hear a well that had followed her all along.

orig.note: Hebrew: Miriam's well, the rabbis' name for the water that followed Israel for her sake.

carryVoice: Your line: Miriam's well. Some gifts are only noticed once they stop. See you tomorrow.
